1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.name: French Defence: St. George Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6.background: The name is borrowed from the St. George Defence, 1.e4 a6, named after England's patron saint, which reaches this position with 2.d4 e6. Its first known game is a simultaneous one in which the English amateur J. Baker beat Wilhelm Steinitz on 11 December 1868.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece towards the centre and guards d4 and e5, keeping the pawn centre flexible instead of committing the c-pawn. It prepares the bishop on d3 and castling, and leaves Black to show whether the queenside advance is really worth the loosening.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a broad three-pawn centre at once and prepares to punish the queenside advance that Black's last move invites: after ...b5 White takes, and the recaptured pawn on b5 stands loose. The price is that the centre is built before any piece is out, so the pawns need support.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, Three Pawn Attack

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, Sanky-George Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5.strategy: A gambit: Black strikes at the c4 pawn and, if White takes, recaptures so as to open the a-file, but the pawn on b5 is then loose and the bishop can win it. An open file and quick development are real but modest compensation, so this is an offbeat try, not a solid choice.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5.strategy: The point of the whole set-up: Black grabs queenside space, takes the a4 and c4 squares from White's pieces and prepares to develop the bishop on the long diagonal against e4. It loosens the queenside, but White cannot easily attack it, since a knight on c3 would meet ...b4.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5.strategy: Accepts the gambit, the principal answer: White takes the pawn and, after Black's recapture, can win the loose pawn on b5 with the f1-bishop. The price is some time, since Black gets an open a-file against the a2 pawn, so White has to consolidate carefully.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5 axb5.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, St. George Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.c4 b5 4.cxb5 axb5.strategy: The natural recapture and the point of the gambit: the a-pawn leaves the a-file, so the rook looks at a2, and White must decide whether the loose pawn on b5 is worth taking. Not recapturing would leave Black a pawn down for nothing.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3.strategy: Puts the bishop on its best diagonal, where it guards e4 in advance against the bishop that Black is about to bring to b7, and eyes the b5 pawn. It does the job a knight on c3 cannot, since that would be driven off by ...b4. White keeps a compact set-up and castling in hand.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5.strategy: Black challenges the centre instead of waiting behind it: the d4 pawn is now attacked by the c-pawn and held only by the knight, because the bishop on d3 shuts in the queen. White has to decide how to meet the tension, and Black gets active play before castling.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3.strategy: Adds a second defender to d4 and keeps the centre intact instead of releasing the tension by capturing on c5. The price is that the queen's knight loses its natural square and has to come out via d2, but White keeps a solid pawn chain and the bishop on its diagonal.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 B.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal against e4, which is what the queenside advance was for. The pawn is held by the bishop on d3, so for now this is pressure, not a threat, but every further attacker on e4 makes it one.

Gets the king to safety before the centre opens. With Black's bishop already aimed at e4 and the d4 pawn under pressure, White wants the king out of the middle and a rook developed, while the bishop and the pawn chain hold the centre together for now.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 B.name: French Defence: St. George Defence, Traditional Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 a6 3.Nf3 b5 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 B.strategy: Brings out the last minor piece with a point: e4 is now attacked twice, by bishop and knight, and defended once, so White has to defend or advance the pawn at once. Black develops while keeping the initiative against the white centre and the space gained on the queenside.
